entries.title: MJ Lenderman on Harry Crews: This Fucked-Up Guy
entries.summary: “I came to the work of Harry Crews through word of mouth. A friend was telling me about this fucked-up guy and his book A Feast of Snakes.”
entries.content:
MJ Lenderman

On Books

I came to the work of Harry Crews through word of mouth about the printed page. When I was still a teenager, I used to stay up late on the front porch of my friend’s house, behind a grocery store near downtown Asheville, North Carolina. We’d attempt to write songs, but mostly we’d get drunk and talk about writing and people who had ﬁgured out how to do it. One time, he was telling me about this fucked-up guy, Harry Crews, and his book A Feast of Snakes, a mid-seventies masterpiece set in Mystic, Georgia.

But I was really hooked when he told me about The Knockout Artist, a book that came a decade later and captured a kid named Eugene Talmadge Biggs who knocked himself out for paying spectators. The next morning, I ordered The Knockout Artist and A Feast of Snakes and a collection featuring his memoir, A Childhood, and the novels The Gypsy’s Curse and Car. I found myself immediately captured by Crews’s books. The dialogue felt so real, the Southernness so pronounced. It was like a warped version of where I was from—not things I had really seen, but scenes I could maybe imagine happening to friends I’d made, like my landlord Gary.

At the time, I was living in a mountain holler called Haw Creek. It was less a band house than a band compound, a couple of houses clustered together where some of my friends and bandmates all lived and worked and barbecued. Gary King owned and lived on the property with us. He’d rattle off dirty limericks in his kitchen and chain-smoke Pall Mall Blues while hooked up to oxygen. He’d park outside our house and lay on the horn until we came out just to talk shit. But he loved us as if we were his grandchildren, and he never raised the rent.

The pandemic came soon, so I stayed home and spent my time playing music and reading and writing. It was—up to that point and maybe even up to right now—the most devoted and formative songwriting phase of my life. Crews helped a lot.

My girlfriend at the time and Wednesday bandmate, Karly Hartzman, had gifted me several of his books that I didn’t have yet, some even signed. And I’d found an index of his interviews that became sort of a self-help guide for writing songs. Crews was born to tenant farmers in Bacon County, Georgia, a name he would have invented for his novels had it not already been real. He had almost no advantages as a young artist, a self-taught kid who had to be tough enough to keep going when no one cared. In those interviews, he said something about how any artistic pursuit involves your ability to withstand failure. That meant so much to me. Crews could seem like such a hard-ass, but that advice was vulnerable and real, a lesson from a guy who had realized that you have to put the idea on the page before you could even start to know if it’s any good.

This was around the time that I was writing what became Boat Songs, the album that led people outside of Asheville to pay a little attention to what I was doing. I knew these songs could look stupid on paper, but they felt right to me. Crews talked, too, about writing as an act of courage. In my own way, singing those songs felt a little like that. I needed that advice to make that music back then, and I still do.

Crews’s very speciﬁc, serious, and silly language was an inspiration, too. Someone is always “hustling his balls” in one of his books, and I think you could write an essay unpacking the implications of those three words. It became a goal to ﬁnd phrases like that. I borrowed or stole from Crews, too. People love to quote a line from my song “Joker Lips” from Manning Fireworks, a batch of stuff that came near the end of my time at Haw Creek: “Every Catholic knows he could have been Pope.” Except, of course, I didn’t write it; Crews did. If you have a ﬁrst edition of Gospel Singer, from William Morrow & Company in 1968, it’s on page 209, toward the middle. I like the way that passage ends, too: “Every man knows that his gift will set him free if he is just lucky enough. Or unlucky enough, depending upon your point of view.”

That bit reminds me of Body, a book that is, at least on the surface, about a bodybuilding standoff between Shereel Dupont and Marvella Washington. Marvella is an imposing Black woman from Detroit; Shereel is a small and sculpted white woman from Waycross, Georgia, so country that her name used to be Dorothy Turnipseed. But Body is barely about them at all. It is, instead, about a stubborn rivalry between Russell “Muscle” Morgan and Wallace “The Wall” Wilson, two over-the-hill coaches who, though still enormous, have only one way left to win a bodybuilding championship: via the women they now command. Muscle so controls Dupont that he forces her to change her name, regulates every drop of water she drinks, keeps her from her family, and determines when she needs to have sex with him. She just wanted to be his secretary; he must make her Ms. Cosmos.

Body is a ridiculous book, every action and name and ﬁgure so exaggerated it can feel like a caricature. But that is what makes Crews so compelling: Even inside this absurd universe, he manages to humanize everyone, to ﬁnd the softness among these hard bodies. How loving can a man named Nail Head be? Very, it turns out. How can a freak-of-nature bodybuilder named Billy Bat ﬁnd the family and romance he didn’t know he’d been looking for with Shereel’s sister, Earline, so addicted to food that she carries around spare pieces of fried chicken? Easily, it turns out. The bodybuilding competition that Crews depicts at the Blue Flamingo is a hilarious shitshow; because it’s Crews, it is also full of heart.

I should offer a warning: Like pretty much every Crews book, Body overﬂows with vile things. The relationship between the white Muscle and the Wall, who is Black, means there’s a lot of racist epithets, ﬁred back and forth like volleys between North and South. And there’s a lot of demeaning sex where the woman has little to no say in the ordeal. It opens with sex so barbaric that Muscle breaks the hotel furniture; the hotel manager—a dork so ashamed of himself he won’t sleep with a woman because it would mean her seeing him without his terrible toupee—hires and ﬁres a series of secretaries he calls only “Miss Beverly,” who give him blowjobs beneath his desk on demand. Crews is a little like a literary highlighter, occasionally using garish colors to show us that this is the way people really can be.

I am not out to spoil Body for you, but I should say something about the end. I’ve talked about how Crews likes to blow things up, to exaggerate and emphasize the messes we make. But the last three pages are a masterstroke of subtlety, a big reveal so nuanced and particular I had to read it a few times to make sure I understood. Every time I have revisited Body since, though, I’ve noticed new clues, breadcrumbs Crews was tossing out to lead us to the inevitability of the end. Following him there didn’t just make me a better reader and writer. Body helped me appreciate how most people—however strange their actions may seem to me—are mostly trying to do their best.

MJ Lenderman was born and raised in Asheville, North Carolina and is a singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist. His albums include the critically acclaimed Boat Songs (2022) and his breakthrough release, Manning Fireworks (2024), which was named one of the year’s best albums by Rolling Stone, Pitchfork, Paste, and The New Yorker.

From the foreword to Harry Crews’s Body, to be published by Penguin Classics on November 10.

entries.title: Election Night in Texas: A Dispatch from the Midterms’ Biggest Sweep
entries.summary: “ ‘So this is a big election for you in Italy?’ I asked her. ‘Oh my God!’ she cried, admonishing me. ‘That is an understatement!’ ”
entries.content:
Sara Van Horn

Dispatch

It was overcast and drizzling just after sunrise, a relative rarity for Austin, and I decided to vote at a nearby theological seminary, hoping a religious spirit might carry into the day. James Talarico, the thirty-seven-year-old state legislator running for the U.S. Senate, is also a Presbyterian seminarian, and was now contesting religious terrain long vacated by Texas Democrats. He has called the relationship binding the governors to the governed a “covenant,” albeit a broken one. He intends, like one barefoot rabbi in the temple courts, to “start flipping tables.” 

Pick the right polling place in Texas and you will be hand-shaked and possibly hip-checked. But the seminary, teeming with UT students, was completely silent—nary a campaign flyer in sight. Still, everyone I asked on the street was hopeful, hopeful, more hopeful. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa was still considered a gubernatorial long shot—with Kalshi traders predicting her victory at just 37% even on Election Day. But even then, it seemed Talarico was going to win, giving the Democrats their first statewide victory in thirty-two years. 

A trio of nonpartisan observers wearing “Election Protection” baseball caps were beaming at me. Anyone with an “I voted” sticker could pick up a free slice from Austin’s beloved Home Slice Pizza (“In Crust We Trust!”). A reporter for an Italian newspaper called Il manifesto assured me that Talarico would make tomorrow’s front page. “So this a big election for you in Italy?” I asked her. “Oh my God!” she cried, admonishing me. “That is an understatement!” 

***

Outside the Texas Union, a bustling polling place just off Austin’s main commercial strip, sacred covenants were held more loosely. A cadre of City Council hopefuls, armed with campaign literature, jostled for position between two fast-moving tributaries: voters searching for the polls and a stream of indifferent college students, who ducked their heads, refused the flyers, and speedwalked to class. The candidates were fearless in their extroversion, forcing the unvoted to slalom quickly between them as if navigating a particularly treacherous obstacle course. Had I voted? Once asked a certain number of times, I started to doubt myself.

Like all sphinxes, city council aspirants will step aside upon hearing the correct answer. Approached by a candidate whose tousled hair I suddenly recognized, I tried my hand. “I just voted for you,” I said, which turned out to be an even better answer. I received a fist bump. The candidate, Rich Heyman, was fired by the University of Texas in 2024 after getting arrested at a pro-Palestine protest. Today, he told me, he was feeling “really good,” at least before one of his opponents nearly slammed into him. She’d rushed over to tell me about her platform, accompanied by visual aids—a collection of personalized animal stickers, each with their own Austin-specific meaning: an armadillo, a salamander, and a bat in bright pastels, surrounding a slogan that read “Make Austin Magical.” I asked them how it felt to be rivals, eliciting an unconvincing side-hug. They are friends, they assure me. Loving your enemy, proclaims Talarico after all, is “good strategic advice.”

The Senate-hopeful’s own enemy was decidedly less easy to love. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton had withstood many scandals: felony securities fraud, cutting sweetheart deals for confessed pedophiles, two extramarital affairs, pocketing a very expensive pen. But “Teflon Ken” seemed impervious; though indicted and impeached (then acquitted), he had remained in public office for over a decade, winning election after election, pushing his party farther to the right, and eliciting a string of bizarre endorsements. One PAC-funded ad intended to tout Paxton’s record on combating human trafficking went viral for effectively communicating the opposite: “When missing posters go up, Ken Paxton takes them down.” As even our president put it, Paxton “may not dress right, he may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen.” None of this has stopped Elon Musk from shelling out at least $212 million in donations to his campaign, helping make this contest the most expensive non-presidential election in the nation’s history.

***

In the afternoon, I headed to a polling place in East Austin flagged as a potential hot spot for ICE activity. I took a Waymo rideshare there and back, closely supervising the steering wheel’s countless micro-adjustments and reflecting on Greg Abbott’s legacy. Over the past eleven years as governor, Abbott has been responsible for one of the “hardest right turns in recent state history,” according to the New York Times. His most infamous triumph is Operation Lone Star, a military initiative which skyrocketed the number of migrant apprehensions along the border, and resulted in a vehicle pursuit death rate eight times higher than the national average.

We pulled to a superbly smooth stop at a traffic light. In September, ICE shot a delivery driver named Wilber Rafael Garces Perez in the back. He was brought to Dell Seton Medical Center at the University of Texas, where he was discharged into ICE custody with the bullet still lodged against his spine. 

But at the George Washington Carver Museum, I learned there had been no sign of ICE all day—in fact, no sign of ICE at polling places in Texas at all (ICE had been given orders, it turned out, to stand down on Election Day). The sun was setting, slicing across the extravagant mural on the museum’s south-facing wall. Two Election Protection volunteers were relaxing on lawn chairs. They’d flown down together from New York: one was a member of the Park Slope Food Coop, the other from Manhattan.

I spoke with more city council hopefuls, who seemed as a cohort to have relaxed over the course of the day. One candidate, Misael Ramos, had been arrested at a recent protest over the shooting of Garces Perez; soon after, he’d secured a national nomination from the Democratic Socialists of America. Misael invited me to his watch party, promising free food, free booze, and a Trump piñata.

***

Misael’s party was not as large as Hinojosa’s or Talarico’s—the latter so oversubscribed that when I emailed for a press credential, his comms team wrote “please do not show up”—but the energy was certainly better. People packed themselves under a backyard tent hung with string lights and screen-printed T-shirts, chattering in English and Spanish, eyes trained on the giant projected television. On a table inside, I found campaign flyers, aforementioned free booze, and containers of taco fillings, scraped clean. Organizers were gathering signatures to end the development of a massive Amazon facility nearby, and the Trump piñata rested on the lawn—still, for now, intact. 

As the results rolled in, the DJ switched between reggaeton and “Party in the U.S.A.” But all music was drowned out by shouting when the Senate race was called for Talarico. “Is Texas blue now?” strangers voiced aloud to each other, incredulous, while others made jubilant phone calls or simply stared at the screen in tears.

When Hinojosa’s victory followed shortly thereafter, there were louder screams, heavier jumping. The two life-long Austinites next to me were stunned. People leaned against each other and sang. “The stars at night! Are big and bright! Deep in the heart! Of Texas…”

Neither Talarico nor Hinojosa support abolishing ICE, we reminded each other, but the defeat of Paxton and Abbott felt like the first of many flipped tables. Just after midnight, as promised, an article appeared in Rome’s Il manifesto, calling Talarico a “fenomeno.”

entries.title: Campaign Literature: Election Day 2026
entries.summary: A selection of Election Day reading from The Paris Review archive.
entries.content:
The Paris Review

From the Archive

Today is Election Day in the United States, the second midterm referendum on the second Trump administration and, given that polls on the West Coast won’t close until eleven this evening, it’s certain to be a long night of scanning the news. If you, like us, have spent the past week, month, year, reading polls, articles, and tea leaves, gaming out the chances that one party may win this or that Senate or House seat, you may, like us, now find yourself in need of some way to kill the next twelve or so hours. Here’s some loosely midterms-adjacent reading from the archive to help you pass the time.

PROSE

A Town Like Kansas

Diane Vreuls

Last night I gave up sex, a political decision. Maria will not leave the convent for Baron von Trapp. She is up on the mountaintop singing. What is the highest point in Kansas?

From issue no. 72 (Winter 1977)

PROSE

Why Visit America

Matthew Baker

There wasn’t anything special about us. We were just an average town. Porch swings, wading pools, split rail fences, pump jacks bobbing for oil on the horizon. Meetings at town hall were well attended, sure, but we weren’t some hotbed of insurgents. We didn’t subscribe to any one brand of politics. We couldn’t even be plotted onto your basic left/right binary. Our town had everything: pro-lifers who supported gay marriage, pro-choicers who opposed gay marriage, climate change deniers who owned solar panels, universal health care campaigners who preferred private insurance, creationists with degrees in biology and geology, loyal conservatives, staunch liberals, moderates, radicals, and ornery retirees whose only real issue was guns. And yet that winter we found ourselves united by a common sentiment. We were fed up with our country. The executives were busy making donations that funded the campaigns of the politicians, the politicians were busy passing laws that protected the interests of the executives, and pretty much nothing else seemed to be getting done. We were antigovernment, we were anticorporate, but mostly we were normal people who couldn’t afford to buy an election and had come to understand that our votes didn’t mean shit. There were libertarians among us who had been pushing to secede for years now, but not until that winter, watching legal forms of graft being flaunted across the country like never before, did our town seriously begin to consider the proposition. The matter soon came to dominate our meetings. We knew that from a certain perspective seceding could be viewed as an act of treason, that it might mean arrest, might mean imprisonment, might even mean execution. And the debate at that final town hall meeting was appropriately heated. Most of us wavered, unsure which way we would vote until the very second those slips of paper got passed around. Several of us were so nervous that we felt faint. Ultimately, however, the decision was unanimous. We would rather face handcuffs, jail, even hanging, than spend another goddamned second living in that broke-down country. We voted to secede.

From issue 230 (Fall 2019)

INTERVIEW

The Art of Fiction No. 237

Dany Laferrière

INTERVIEWER

Your mother once compared you to your father by saying that you have a terrible appetite for life.

LAFERRIÈRE

Yes. My father was a politician and a political activist and a dandy. He would change shirts at least twice or three times a day. He was the youngest-ever mayor of Port-au-Prince.

From issue no. 222 (Fall 2017)

THE DAILY

For Our Cause Is Just

Lydia Moland

“I am not yet prepared to believe that the people of this republic are corrupt enough to choose by fair and honest votes, such a blot upon humanity as Andrew Jackson,” Lydia Maria Child wrote to her new mother-in-law in the early months after Jackson’s election in 1828 … She did not contest the election: the votes had been “fair and honest.” Why, then, did she call her fellow citizens “corrupt”?

From July 2017

THE DAILY

Joan Quigley, Ronald Reagan’s Guide to the Stars

Jessica Weisberg

“Virtually every major move and decision the Reagans made during my time as White House Chief of Staff was cleared in advance with this woman in San Francisco who drew up horoscopes to make certain that the planets were in a favorable alignment for the enterprise,” writes Don Regan, President Reagan’s chief of staff, in his memoir, For the Record. Regan kept a color-coded calendar on his desk, with “good” days highlighted in green and “bad” days highlighted in red. Here’s the calendar for the first few months of 1986:

Jan 16–23 very bad

Jan 20 nothing outside the WH—possible attempt

Feb 20–26 be careful

March 7–14 bad period

March 10–14 no outside activity

March 16 very bad

March 21 no

March 27 no

March 12–19 no trips exposure

March 19–25 no public exposure

April 1 careful

April 11 careful

April 17 careful

April 21–28 stay home

From June 2018

INTERVIEW

The Art of Fiction No. 7

Joyce Cary

INTERVIEWER

Are the political aspects of your work controlled by the same ideas?

CARY

Religion is organized to satisfy and guide the soul—politics does the same thing for the body. Of course they overlap—this is a very rough description. But the politician is responsible for law, for physical security, and in a world of tumult, of perpetual conflict, he has the alternatives, roughly again, of persuading people or shooting them. In the democracies, we persuade. And this gives great power to the spellbinder, the artist in words, the preacher, the demagogue, whatever you call him. Rousseau, Marx, Tolstoy, these were great spellbinders—as well as Lacordaire. My Nimmo is a typical spellbinder. Bonser was a spellbinder in business, the man of imagination. He was also a crook, but so are many spellbinders. Poets have started most of the revolutions, especially nationalist revolutions. On the other hand, life would die without poets, and democracy must have its spellbinders.

From issue no. 7 (Fall–Winter 1954–1955)

THE DAILY

A Number of Reasons I’ve Been Depressed Lately

David Sedaris

On Inauguration Day, I am in Seattle. Late in the afternoon, my old friend Lyn sends me a photo of an anti-Trump sticker someone found in Japan. It’s cleverly designed: three peaks that on second glance turn out to be Trump sandwiched between two Klansmen. I want to write back and say, Ha, but instead, as a joke, I respond, “Dear Lyn, I’m sorry you’re so opposed to change, or too small-minded to move past your narrow assumptions. In the future, I’d appreciate your keeping things like this to yourself. David”

A minute later, I send a follow-up email that says, “Just kidding.” And it bounces back, as do the next three emails I send. She’s blocked me! I realize. After thirty-eight years of friendship!

From June 2017

INTERVIEW

The Art of Poetry No. 102

Claudia Rankine

RANKINE

The relationship between public engagement and private thought are inseparable for me. I worked on Citizen on and off for almost ten years. I wrote the first piece in response to Hurricane Katrina. I was profoundly moved by the events in New Orleans as they unfolded. John and I taped the CNN coverage of the storm without any real sense of what we intended to do with the material. I didn’t think, obviously, that I was working on Citizen.

But for me, there is no push and pull. There’s no private world that doesn’t include the dynamics of my political and social world. When I am working privately, my process includes a sense of what is happening in the world. Today, for example, I feel incredibly drained. And probably you do, too.

From issue no. 219 (Winter 2016)

ART

Amazing But True

Joe Brainard

From issue no. 53 (Winter 1972)

POETRY

Bangor

Timothy Donnelly

Poor Aunt Midge, who: 1. refused to change

however times did; 2. spread a) expansive memories

through Maine and b) jarred orange marmalade on scones;

having lived: 3. equally for a) pearls and b) perms,

and 4. beside the phone, one longish life led out in Bangor,

one brain gone stale as loaves of store-bought bread,

has died. December twenty-four and “she is dead”

From issue no. 153 (Winter 1999)

INTERVIEW

The Art of Biography No. 5

Robert Caro

CARO

I thought, There’s one guy who’s with Lyndon Johnson most of the day, and it’s not his campaign manager, it’s his chauffeur! Because in the Texas Hill Country, a lot of anything is driving—that’s ninety percent of the time. His chauffeur was a guy named Carroll Keach. He lived in some place outside Corpus Christi, and it was hard to get to. It was, like, a 180-mile drive or something. But I kept going back to him.

He wasn’t a loquacious Texan, he was a laconic Texan. I would ask, What was Johnson doing between campaign stops? And he would say something like, Oh, he was just sitting there in the backseat. I just had to keep asking him questions. I mean, you’re driving, Carroll, and Lyndon Johnson is in the backseat? What was he doing in the backseat? Finally, he told me that Johnson often would be talking to himself. So I’d call and say, Carroll, when you said he was talking to himself, what was he saying? Finally, Carroll told me, It was like he was having discussions with himself about whether he had had a successful day, and if he had made a good impression on voters or not … Johnson would say, Boy, wasn’t that dumb! You know you just lost that ballot box. You lost it, and you need it. And he would talk out—rehearse, over and over, out loud, what he would say to the voters in that precinct the next time.

From issue no. 2016 (Spring 2016)

THE DAILY

Texas Forever

Adam Wilson

I’m a Reagan baby, a product of recession, later reared in the economically secure Clinton nineties, in a McMansioned suburb of the Eastern Seaboard. Our athletes—statuesque Celtics and sinewy Red Sox—were billboarded, televised, and extra-life-sized for us to admire as we turned into populist fist-pumpers in the soft reflection of our screens.

From July 2011

INTERVIEW

The Art of Theater No. 2

Arthur Miller

I always drew a lot of inspiration from politics, from one or another kind of national struggle. You live in the world even though you only vote once in a while. It determines the extensions of your personality. I lived through the McCarthy time, when one saw personalities shifting and changing before one’s eyes, as a direct, obvious result of a political situation. And had it gone on, we would have gotten a whole new American personality—which in part we have … Such a pall of fright was laid upon us that it truly deflected the American mind. It’s part of a paranoia which we haven’t escaped yet. Good God, people still give their lives for it; look what we’re doing in the Pacific.

From issue no. 38 (Summer 1966)

INTERVIEW

The Art of Fiction No. 236

Ali Smith

INTERVIEWER

Are you a nationalist?

SMITH

I’m not.

From issue no. 221 (Summer 2017)

POETRY

Letter from Kitty Dukakis: Between the Election and the Breakdown

Rick Adang

They called it a landslide as though

everything shifted and the weak

and strong alike were buried alive.

Not true. We simply came home.

From issue no. 130 (Spring 1994)

entries.title: Belgrade Diary: Election Day in Serbia
entries.summary: The Serbian Progressive Party's leader, Aleksandar Vučić, finally had a real competitor in Student List.
entries.content:
Lily Lynch

Dispatch

October 25, 2026

6:30 A.M.

On Election Day, all normal time stopped. From early in the morning, friends sent me footage of lines snaking around buildings, through parks, down city blocks. A friend back in California sent me photos of a party at a café near the Serbian consulate in Los Angeles, with music, dancing, barbecue. A few weeks earlier, the Serbian Republic Electoral Commission had announced that the country’s large diaspora would be allowed to vote only during Serbia’s domestic polling hours. This meant that Serbian voters in other countries and time zones would have to travel to their embassy or consulate at odd hours or in the middle of the night to cast their ballots. The last-minute rule change was widely interpreted as an attempt by the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) to undercut its insurgent rival, Student List (SL). The Serbian diaspora was known to favor the opposition.

One friend wanted to make a bet: “The turnout is going to be record-breaking,” he wrote. “And SL will win by a landslide.” I was cautiously optimistic, but not a true believer. Though not Serbian myself, I’d been reporting on the nation for more than a decade; I’ve covered countless Serbian elections over the past fourteen years and was in Serbia for the SNS’s ascent to power in 2012. The party’s leader, Aleksandar Vučić, also the country’s erstwhile president and premier, had always managed to outsmart us. Without fail, he had either won outright or massaged the vote to his liking when he hadn’t: a little ballot-stuffing here, a little Gogolian resurrection of dead voters there, along with some voter intimidation and paying the poor and marginalized for their votes. Why should this time be any different?

If anything, this time would be worse, perhaps far worse. Vučić finally had a real competitor in SL, a new outfit that had emerged out of two years of student protests, and which, according to at least some polls, enjoyed more popular support than SNS. None of the names on SL’s slate were those of students, but nor were they professional politicians. All of them—professors, doctors, actors, engineers, athletes—had been selected via plenum. The group therefore represented an entirely novel approach to national politics. If it managed to pull off a win, an age-old status quo would come to an end.

I had barely slept. In the run-up to Election Day, pro-Vučić media outlets said that violence or even civil war would break out. Many were expecting at least some bloodshed. A worried friend bought me a neon-yellow high-vis reflector vest that he hoped would identify me as press, though I was later reminded that this could just as easily make me a target. There were other foreboding signs going into the day: a Red Star Belgrade football match was scheduled for four that afternoon, meaning that the cantankerous and marauding sports fans and for-hire brutes known as Delije, with whom Vučić had close ties, would be out on the streets. An eleventh-hour change to legal procedures at the Belgrade Higher Court seemed to portend mass arrests.

I dressed, trying to recall the last time I’d had anything to eat. It had been the previous afternoon. I still had no appetite.

8 A.M.

I decided to walk thirty minutes to meet my friend Sonja at her polling station in Dorćol, the city’s oldest neighborhood. In Belgrade, the previous day had been immaculate: autumnal, sunny, and crisp. Now it was gray.

There were more people out on the streets than usual, but not by much. When I walked past the nearest polling station and saw just a few people out front, my faith wavered. Perhaps all the jubilant reports I’d received from friends of long lines were nothing more than their wishful thinking, people only seeing what they wanted to see. Most likely, this time would be just like all the rest. It was foolish to have gotten my hopes up.

I made my way down to Slavija, a large traffic roundabout surrounding a public fountain. A jumbo campaign ad of Vučić stared down at me from the facade of a tall building. The ubiquity of his face—on buildings, on the cover of every lurid tabloid, on state television—seemed almost cartoonishly authoritarian.

As I approached Novi Dvor, the president’s office, I saw that the police had erected barricades, preventing passage by foot or car. A smattering of officers was milling around. Mustering my most confident Serbian, I asked one if I could pass through. “I live a few blocks up,” I told him, “off of Terazije.” Wordlessly, with an air of exhaustion, he made make an opening in the barriers and waved me along. I allowed myself to wonder whether state power would fold with so little resistance later that night.

9 A.M.

Sonja met me in front of her polling station, the commerce school on Hilandarska Street. Inside, there was a flurry of activity but, dishearteningly, no voting queue.

After Sonja cast her vote, we walked to Palilula Market, where we had heard there was going to be an informal election party. Despite the hour, some around us were drinking shots of rakija, a popular kind of brandy. My phone lit up with notifications detailing a record early-voter turnout. By nine, the numbers were twice those of the previous election, in 2023. We considered whether the showing could somehow be explained by the end of daylight savings at three that same morning.

11 A.M.

I took one of the city’s antiquated red trams down Bulevar kralja Aleksandra to Zvezdara, a neighborhood just south of downtown Belgrade, where I met a mobile election-monitoring team for SL. To guard against electoral subterfuge, SL had dispatched them to the general vicinity of specific polling sites. They were trained to identify expected forms of interference, from garden-variety intimidation to the so-called Bulgarian Train, a method of rigging votes. By the time I arrived, they had just diffused a tense situation with a local SNS-backed thug.

Unaccountably, the mobile team’s spirits seemed high, as though the incident had hardly bothered them. I received a text saying that by noon, turnout was 34.4%.

1:30 P.M.

The mobile team dropped me off on Bulevar kralja Aleksandra, and I decided to walk its length back toward downtown. At some point, my appetite returned, so I stopped off at an Italian restaurant that I had patronized countless times in my more than fifteen years of coming to Serbia. Unsure what to do after lunch, I returned to my apartment. The long wait for the initial results was unbearable, so I thought I’d try to sleep through part of it.

3 P.M.

I couldn’t sleep. My mood had turned, the cautious optimism of the morning fading to let dread creep back in. The high turnout of the morning had leveled off, one friend wrote. It was still much higher than in elections past, but would it be enough? For SL to win, it would need greater voter participation than this. A friend texted to reassure me: “Things were just slowing down for lunch, which is as expected. Just wait.”

4 P.M.

I walked to the headquarters of the Center for Research, Transparency, and Accountability (CRTA), an election watchdog, to attend a press conference. Raša Nedeljkov, the center’s director, told us that the morning turnout was indeed historic. But by afternoon, he confirmed, things had petered out somewhat. He read off a litany of irregularities: there were widespread problems with the ultraviolet lamps and ultraviolet spray used to guard against repeat voting, and at least two locations, election observers had been attacked. After the press conference, I paced around the office, drinking perhaps too much instant coffee.

6 P.M.

I left CRTA shortly after dark. I wanted to see what was happening at Pionirski Park, which sits adjacent to the Republic Electoral Commission. What I saw there made my stomach turn: riot police in full gear were amassing in the park, already pitch black with the streetlights turned off. This, I thought, was the clearest signal yet that Vučić planned to declare victory no matter the polling figures—and that he was prepared to use force.

7:30 P.M.

With a sense of restlessness, I returned to CRTA, where I accepted the offer of a British journalist from the Times to accompany him and his fixer to the SL headquarters. For security reasons, or so the story went, SL was based all the way out in New Belgrade, on the opposite side of the Sava River. New Belgrade was built entirely after the Second World War, a showcase of Yugoslav socialist brutalism. The SL base of operations was located somewhere amid its imposing concrete blocks.

As we left CRTA in a taxi, we saw a large group of men in black walking toward Pionirski Park. “Those don’t look like students,” the Times journalist offered. There was no mistaking who they were. These were thugs in the employ of the state authorities, their henchmen for carrying out dirty work. Our car sped away before we saw exactly what their business was, but it was almost certainly something violent.

In New Belgrade, the SL offices were in a state of pandemonium. Journalists from all over the world had descended on the scene, jostling for an electrical outlet for their equipment or just a place to sit. People were piled on top of one another. It seemed we had all had the same idea. It wouldn’t be long—just thirty minutes—before the polls closed; the first batch of results would come in just a little after that. I doubted whether it was worthwhile to wait things out from SL, where the frenzy and commotion were distracting. And I wasn’t so sure that I wanted to ring in the victory, no matter whose it would be, among so many members of the media.

8:46 P.M.

Back at my apartment, I got a word from a well-connected contact, who informed me that the U.S. embassy had congratulated SL on its victory in the parliamentary elections. I wasn’t sure whether to believe it; there were no major sources claiming triumph for SL, and it seemed unwise to place much too stock in one informant. Better to be agnostic about the results until the polls were in.

9:23 P.M.

I received another message from the same source: the U.S. embassy had reportedly congratulated SL’s representatives, but had told them to hold off on announcing victory until Vučić held his own press conference. That press conference, said my source, would begin in the next five minutes.

Meanwhile, pro-Vučić television stations began announcing their preliminary election “results,” projecting that SNS would win by a landslide, securing 54.21% of the vote to Student List’s 36.85%.

9:30 P.M.

I heard hollers from outside, coming from many voices all at once. Seconds later, I received a message from a friend: Vučić had conceded defeat.

Instinctively, I tore my door open and ran outside. Everyone else had apparently done the same. I saw a group of women sobbing in the street; when they caught sight of me, they came over to fold me into their embrace. For years, Western diplomats had justified their support for Vučić by saying that Serbs love a strongman, as though it were a recognized aspect of the national character. Now, as if to contradict the old brocard, the country had elected a leaderless movement to power.

I ambled down to Slavija Square, where people were just starting to gather. We walked into traffic. Drivers left their cars in the street to join the celebration. Young men set off a deafening round of fireworks. My ears ringing, I bumped into a teenager with a shaved head. Instead of apologizing and moving on, we hugged and jumped up and down, screaming. One of Belgrade’s red trams had been stopped in its tracks and was now being taken over by the people, who hung out of its windows screaming pobeda!—“victory!”

Everyone I met kept repeating the length of Vučić’s reign—“fourteen years!”—in disbelief. I thought about all that had transpired in that time: the relationships that had ended, the people who had died, the activists whose idealism had collapsed into cynicism and despair, the many people who had left the country, vowing never to return.

I stumbled around for an hour or two—time had long since stopped making sense—and decided to go back to my apartment. I still had to report on these developments, produce an account of things that would keep me tethered to the outside world.

When I got home, I read the messages in my email inbox. My friend Tara had written, “Honestly, genuinely, in the back of my mind I think Vučić is pulling a fast one on us somehow.” Every third person I talked to expressed similar misgivings: that somehow, he wasn’t really finished, that he would find a way to sabotage the moment and seize power again, that it was all an elaborate Machiavellian stunt, that it wasn’t really over. I could understand why. For those who’d lived with his omnipresence for so long, it was hard to believe that he was gone.

Lily Lynch is a foreign-affairs writer and the co-founder and editor-in-chief of  Balkanist Magazine.
